recon.potential_tc_confusion: Table 2 lists plant parameters by CO2 concentration columns (370, 470, 570) - straightforward. Risk of confusion between the two elevated treatments when extracting separately. Also note that 470 ppm showed stronger flowering response than 570 ppm, which is unusual and should not be misinterpreted as a T/C swap.
recon.sample_size_source: Ten plants were put into each of 3 growth cabinets... Plants were rotated between chambers every 2 weeks
recon.extraction_guidance: Primary mineral concentration data are in Figure 3a (leaf and stem tissue separately, 5 elements each: N, P, K, Ca, Mg) expressed as mg/g dry weight. Figure 3b shows total element pools (mg/plant) as a proxy for uptake. Both figures show means with 95% CI bars for three CO2 levels (370, 470, 570 ppm). Extract leaf tissue concentrations from Fig 3a as the primary outcome (most relevant to dilution hypothesis). Note that leaf and stem must be treated as separate tissue types. Statistical significance: leaf N, P, Mg all P<0.001; K and Ca P<0.01 (ANOVA). For pools (Fig 3b): Ca and Mg P<0.05; N, P, K not significant. Table 1 is RAINWATER INPUT composition - do not confuse with plant tissue data. Table 2 contains only biomass/growth data. The C:N ratio in leaf tissue is reported in text (not figures): 40.1, 44.3, 51.7 for 370, 470, 570 ppm respectively - can be used as supplementary data point. n=10 per treatment. Values must be read from bar graphs; no numerical tables for mineral data exist in this paper.
